title: Pharmacokinetics in Neonatal Medicine

paragraphs.text: 47 Pharmacokinetics in Neonatal Medicine
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The safe and effective use of medications in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) requires an understanding of the principles of pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) that guide individual dosing and aim to provide drug exposures designed for the best clinical outcomes and lowest risk of adverse effects. Significant differences in neonatal physiology affect drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination. Therefore the PK of drugs in neonates is unique and cannot be extrapolated from older children or adults (for excellent comprehensive reviews see references 1–3).1–3 Biologic variation among infants in the NICU is extensive: infant’s weight varies at least 10-fold (0.5–5 kg), gestational age at birth varies between 22 and 42 weeks, and postnatal age typically ranges from 1 to 150 days. Infants are undergoing dramatic changes in body size, body composition, cardiac output and perfusion, renal and hepatic function, and ontogeny (agerelated maturation) of drug metabolizing enzymes. This means that infants in the NICU will exhibit wide variations in drug exposures, and care providers often need to consider dose adjustments. Developmental changes in organ systems also influence safety and efficacy of drugs used in infants. Basic knowledge of PK and PD can explain rational dosing across a broad spectrum of prematurity, clinical conditions, treatment interventions, and drug classes. The interplay of PK and PD relationships allows clinicians to target specific drug concentrations that have been associated with therapeutic efficacy (Fig. 47.1).
paragraphs.heading: CHI D. HORNIK AND KELLY C. WADE

paragraphs.text: Anti-infective drugs are the most common class of drugs used in the NICU and provide a useful context to understand basic principles of PK and PD (see Fig. 47.1). The goals of antimicrobial therapy are simple: eradicate the pathogen, minimize toxicity, and prevent emergence of resistant organisms.4,5 The PK of a drug explains the dose-concentration relationship, whereas the PD of a drug explains the relationship between the concentration of the drug in the body and the therapeutic or toxic response. With basic PK knowledge, clinicians can predict the concentration of drug in the plasma at a given time after a given dose. If a specific drug plasma concentration is known, then
paragraphs.heading: CHI D. HORNIK AND KELLY C. WADE

paragraphs.text: dose modification can be determined to provide the desired drug concentration in that infant.
paragraphs.heading: PD

paragraphs.text: This chapter reviews basic PK and PD principles and the mathematical formulas that enable clinicians to predict an infant’s dose-exposure relationship.1–3,6 Both drug- and infant-specific factors can explain the variation in drug exposures among term and preterm infants in the NICU. Optimal dosing in neonates requires that clinicians understand the basic principles of the PK and the developmental and physiologic basis for this variation in drug exposures. Examples illustrate the use of simple PK calculations to predict differences in drug exposures among very preterm and term neonates.
paragraphs.heading: PD

paragraphs.text: Drug disposition describes how drugs enter and exit the body and explains how concentrations in the body change
paragraphs.heading: Drug Disposition Explains Drug Exposure Over Time: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion

paragraphs.text: over time (Figs. 47.2 and 47.3). Four basic processes explain the disposition of drugs through the body: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. These processes are affected by chemical properties of the drug, patient-specific physiology, body composition, developmental maturation, and pathophysiology relating to disease state. Applying PK principles in neonates requires an understanding of drug disposition and the impact of both developmental pharmacology and patient-specific physiology.1–3
paragraphs.heading: Drug Disposition Explains Drug Exposure Over Time: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion

paragraphs.text: Absorption specifically refers to the process of drug transfer from its site of administration to the bloodstream (see Fig. 47.2). Drugs typically enter the body via intravenous (IV), enteral (per oral, PO), intramuscular (IM), intrapulmonary, subcutaneous, or percutaneous routes and are then absorbed into the circulation as free drug. The route of administration affects the concentration of the drug over time (see Fig. 47.3). Bioavailability of a drug refers to the fraction of the administered dose that reaches the circulation but does not consider the rate of drug absorption. Bioavailability is determined by comparing the respective areas under the plasma concentration curves (AUC) after a non- IV form of administration with the AUC after an IV administration. IV administration of a drug, with the exception of dosing formulations of prodrugs, provides the most consistent, reliable absorption into the circulation and therefore defines a bioavailability of 100%. Prodrugs, often designed to improve poor bioavailability and absorption, are inactive
paragraphs.heading: Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

paragraphs.text: until they are converted into an active form through transformative processes in the body.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

paragraphs.text: For enteral medications, the bioavailability depends on biochemical properties of the drug, the formulation, and patient-specific factors such as gastric acidity, gastric emptying time, and intestinal absorption and transit time. Bioavailability is reduced by incomplete absorption and by increased first-pass metabolism as the drug enters the portal circulation, where it can be metabolized in the liver before reaching the systemic circulation. The degree of first-pass metabolism plays an important role in bioavailability. For enteral midazolam, a physiologic population PK model demonstrated a higher bioavailability of 92% in preterm
paragraphs.heading: Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

paragraphs.text: infants compared with 30% for adults, a finding explained by reduced first-pass metabolism in preterm infants.7 Drugs administered enterally enter the circulation more slowly than IV bolus-administered drugs and therefore achieve a lower maximum drug concentration (Cmax) later after administration (see Fig. 47.3). Drug-specific dose adjustment is needed when converting IV to enteral formulations to achieve consistent exposure.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

paragraphs.text: Neonates have unique absorption properties that impact drug concentrations after enteral administration.1–3 Although the ontogeny of gastric acid production and secretion is not fully understood, neonates with reduced gastric acidity have increased absorption of acid-labile molecules (penicillin) and decreased absorption of weak organic acids (phenytoin, phenobarbital). Frequent and continuous oral feedings in infants may result in higher gastric pH and impact the absorption of these drugs. Slower gastric emptying time and intestinal motility among preterm infants can change the time to absorb the drug and amount of drug absorbed. Enteral absorption often improves as infants become older. Absorption of enteral medications is often decreased in infants with GI pathology or changes in perfusion to the GI system. Anticipating differences in bioavailability helps guide dose adjustment when converting between IV and PO routes of administration.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

paragraphs.text: Bioavailability after IM and percutaneous (topical or transdermal) administration can be affected by tissue mass, perfusion, drug permeability, and surface area. In neonates, reduced muscle perfusion and contractility can limit absorption after IM administration.3 The percutaneous absorption of the drug is directly related to the degree of skin hydration and relative surface area and inversely related to the thickness of the stratum corneum. Percutaneous application of medications in preterm infants can lead to large systemic drug exposures given their increased skin perfusion secondary to larger surface area, higher water content, and thin stratum corneum.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

paragraphs.text: Distribution refers to the process by which drugs move from the central circulation through various compartments and peripheral tissues in the body according to physiochemical properties such as the molecular size, ionization constant, and relative hydrophilic/lipophilic properties (see Fig. 47.2). The central compartment typically refers to the vascular space with rapid distribution to the heart, kidney, and liver. From the central compartment, drugs distribute at a slower rate to the peripheral compartment(s), which can include brain, fat, and muscle. From the peripheral tissues, drugs traverse back into the central compartment to be eliminated. Drug distribution depends on drug-specific factors (molecular size, ionization constant, relative hydrophilic/ lipophilic properties, protein binding) and infant-specific factors (body composition, membrane/tissue permeability, cardiac output). Distribution is an important concept to understanding PK because it relates to the maximum drug
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution and Volume of Distribution

paragraphs.text: concentration after a given dose and the volume of distribution (Vd). The kinetics of drug transfer to and from the peripheral and central compartments also affects the kinetics of drug excretion and the shape of the drug concentration curve over time.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution and Volume of Distribution

paragraphs.text: The apparent Vd for a drug is defined as the hypothetical fluid volume through which the drug is dispersed. It is calculated by dividing the total amount of drug given by the concentration of drug in plasma (Table 47.1, Eq. [3]). This proportionality constant links the dose of the drug to the measured concentration in that compartment. Vd does not refer to any physiologic compartment or the blood volume. Instead, Vd relates to the hypothetical volume of the total compartment that explains the concentration of the drug achieved after administering a given amount.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution and Volume of Distribution

paragraphs.text: Vd is one of the most important parameters of the PK of drugs and is a major factor in determining drug exposure after a given dose.2,3 Understanding the factors that contribute to variation in Vd is helpful in determining the optimal dose of a medication to achieve a desired peak concentration (Cmax) in a specific patient. An infant with a higher Vd will have a lower peak concentration of drug in circulation. High Vd can indicate that the infant has an increase in total body water and extracellular fluid or that the drug has a wide distribution to peripheral tissues where it might be sequestered. Gentamicin is a highly polar, hydrophilic molecule that distributes readily in extracellular fluid. Relative to term infants, preterm infants have a higher body water content and therefore require a higher dose of gentamicin per their body weight to achieve the same peak concentration as a term infant.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution and Volume of Distribution

paragraphs.text: Plasma protein binding can have significant effects on distribution. Drugs that exhibit high protein-binding capacity often have smaller Vd because they bind to plasma proteins and are maintained in the circulation. Protein binding is also affected by availability of binding proteins, differences of binding capacity among different proteins, and increases in bilirubin or free fatty acids that can reduce drug protein binding. Drugs that remain unbound to proteins (“free” drugs) are not only pharmacologically active but also more available for metabolism and/or elimination. Neonates typically have a higher proportion of “free drug” compared to total drug because of decreased concentrations of albumin, alpha-1 acid glycoprotein, and plasma globulins compared to adults.2,3 Lower amounts of these binding proteins can result in toxicities associated with higher free drug concentrations. Increased concentrations of bilirubin and free fatty acids can also increase the amount of “free drug” because they compete with drugs for protein binding.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Distribution and Volume of Distribution

paragraphs.text: Biotransformation is the process that typically converts lipophilic drug molecules into more polar, hydrophilic derivatives (see Fig. 47.2).2,3,8 Polar metabolites are less likely to diffuse across cell membranes and distribute into peripheral tissues and are more likely to be eliminated from the body. At birth, sulfation is relatively developed; however, acetylation and glucuronidation are not well developed.2,3,8 Glucuronidation is an important pathway for metabolism of morphine and acetaminophen.9 Morphine clearance (CL) is low in neonates, and different morphine-glucuronide metabolites predominate because glucuronidation pathways are underdeveloped at birth.10 In neonates receiving acetaminophen, sulfation compensates for some of the glucuronidation deficiencies at birth such that sulfate-conjugated metabolites become the predominant excreted form.9 Glucuronidation capacity subsequently increases after birth with postnatal and postmenstrual age, resulting in changes in the metabolism of drugs among infants in the NICU.2,3
paragraphs.heading: Follow First-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: In general, neonates exhibit reduced hepatic metabolism, which leads to increased drug concentrations, delayed CL, and a longer half-life of medications that require biotransformation before excretion.2,3 This delay in hepatic metabolism is caused by decreases in production in many drug-metabolizing enzymes and limited uptake of drugs into hepatocytes. Metabolism may also be enhanced or impaired by environmental, genetic, and physiologic factors. Environmental influences include concomitant medications that may induce or inhibit drug-metabolizing enzymes; fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, whereas phenobarbital induces CYP2B and CYP3A. The cytochrome P450 genes also exhibit wide genetic variation explained by single nucleotide polymorphisms that can diminish or enhance enzyme activity and significantly affect drug metabolism. For example, codeine is metabolized to morphine by CYP2D6; children whose CYP2D6 genotype leads to ultra-rapid metabolism of codeine can experience morphine toxicity. Case reports describe morphine toxicity in breastfeeding infants whose mothers expressed the CYP2D6 ultra-rapid genotype and were prescribed codeine.11 Other factors affecting hepatic metabolism include uptake of drugs into hepatocytes, hepatic blood flow, body temperature, and disease states affecting perfusion.
paragraphs.heading: Follow First-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: Hepatic processes change rapidly over the first month, so dose adjustment is often necessary with advancing postnatal and postmenstrual age. Fentanyl is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4-mediated N-dealkylation to norfentanyl. Fentanyl elimination depends on liver blood flow, hepatic uptake, and CYP3A4 activity. Not surprisingly, fentanyl PK is highly variable in neonates; half-life ranges from 317 to 1266 minutes, and CL increases threefold in the first 2 weeks of life.12 In the first 48 hours after birth, fentanyl CL increases 40% between infants born at 29 weeks’ gestation compared with 41 weeks’ gestation.13
paragraphs.heading: Follow First-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: Understanding the differences in drug metabolism is important to knowing drug exposures in neonates; if neonates cannot effectively metabolize a drug, then higher concentrations of the active drug can potentiate effects
paragraphs.heading: Follow First-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: of the drug or lead to toxicity. In the absence of specific drug-metabolizing enzymes, neonates may use alternative pathways and produce different metabolites with different activity or toxicity profiles. As drug-metabolizing capacity improves with age, higher doses are necessary to achieve desired concentration and response.
paragraphs.heading: Follow First-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: The excretion of active drugs or their metabolites is the process by which drugs are removed from the body. Drug excretion primarily occurs through the kidney and liver (see Fig. 47.2).1–3 The kidney uses three mechanisms of drug excretion: glomerular filtration, active secretion through the proximal tubules, or distal tubule reabsorption. Glomerular filtration is very low in the first few days after birth and increases with hemodynamic changes and improved renal perfusion. Glomerular filtration also increases with gestational age; preterm infants typically have delayed renal CL and a longer half-life compared with term infants.1–3 Disease states common in critically ill newborns, such as neonatal encephalopathy, sepsis, acute kidney injury, and congenital heart disease, all have been associated with reduced glomerular filtration and reduced drug excretion.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Excretion

paragraphs.text: Tubular processes related to drug secretion and reabsorption are also important to renal elimination, yet incompletely understood, particularly in neonates. Drug secretion in the proximal tubules uses transport systems that typically eliminate organic anions. Secretion transporter proteins secrete drugs that are conjugated with glucuronic acid, glycine, and sulfate, such as penicillin or furosemide. Tubular secretion is less developed in newborns, thereby partially explaining the prolonged half-life of penicillin and furosemide.1–3 Membrane transporters in the distal tubule can actively reabsorb drugs from the tubular lumen back into the systemic circulation. Tubular reabsorption is also delayed in neonates. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) typically improves with maturation faster than tubular mechanisms.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Excretion

paragraphs.text: The liver uses four mechanisms of drug excretion: drug metabolism, excretion into bile, fecal elimination, and enterohepatic recirculation. Hepatic drug elimination can be dependent on hepatic blood flow and the metabolic capacity of liver. Patients with hepatic insufficiency have decreased elimination of drugs because of alterations in protein levels and protein binding, decreased liver blood flow, decreased uptake into hepatocytes, and altered hepatic enzymatic reaction. Patients with hepatic insufficiency, however, exhibit marked variability in drug metabolism and elimination. Infants with hepatic insufficiency typically benefit from lower doses of drugs that are eliminated by hepatic biotransformation and therapeutic drug monitoring when possible.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Excretion

paragraphs.text: Regardless of excretion mechanism, the rate at which drugs are eliminated from the circulation is essential to the PK properties of drug CL, elimination rate constant (Kel), and half-life (T1⁄2) (see formulas in Table 47.1, Eqs. [4, 6]). Drug CL is defined as the volume of blood from which all drug is removed per unit time; Kel represents the elimination
paragraphs.heading: Drug Excretion

paragraphs.text: rate constant, in other words, the slope of the drug concentration time curve on a semi-logarithmic plot; and T1⁄2 is defined as the time it takes to clear half of the drug from plasma. CL can be affected by body weight, body surface area, cardiac output, hepatic function, renal function, plasma protein binding, concomitant medications, and variation in the expression of drug metabolizing enzymes. At steady state, drug input is equal to drug elimination and therefore the dose given (dose/interval) is equal to the amount of drug removed (CL × drug concentration at steady state).
paragraphs.heading: Drug Excretion

paragraphs.text: Drug disposition (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) exhibits marked complexity and interpatient variability in neonates given the infant’s specific differences in body size and composition, maturation, postnatal age, organ function, and clinical disease (pathophysiology).1–3 In neonates, the Vd is often higher for hydrophilic drugs, leading to a lower maximum drug concentration. Elimination (Kel) and CL are often slower because of reduced rates of biotransformation and renal elimination. The expected changes in drug metabolism with maturation can be highly variable and depend on the drug, the metabolic pathways, and clinical disease. The PK characteristics of drugs, specifically Vd and CL, need to be studied across a broad range of prematurity, body compositions, postnatal and postmenstrual ages, and disease states.
paragraphs.heading: Drug Disposition Impacts Pharmacokinetic Characteristics of Drugs in Neonates

paragraphs.text: Pharmacokinetic models describe the mathematical relationship between the dose of a medication administered to a patient and the drug concentration over time after a given dose (Figs. 47.4 and 47.5). These drug concentration-versus-time
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacokinetic Models Describe Concentration of Drug Over Time

paragraphs.text: curves describe the disposition of drugs through the body and are the basis for the mathematical models (kinetics of decay) that predict individual drug concentrations over time in specific patients. Drug concentrations are typically only available from the blood and serve as a surrogate for drug concentration at sites of action to correlate with pharmacologic response.
paragraphs.heading: TIME

paragraphs.text: The drug-concentration-over-time graphs in Fig. 47.4 depict the rate of elimination of a drug from the body on a linear and semi-logarithmic plot. Most drugs follow firstorder kinetics, and mathematical equations in Table 47.1 are appropriate for drugs that are eliminated using properties of first-order kinetics.1,6 For drugs that follow first-order kinetics, a constant percentage of drug is metabolized over time. Because the rate of elimination (Kel) is proportional to the amount of drug in the body, a larger amount of drug is removed per unit time initially and a smaller amount of drug is removed when concentrations are low. When drugs follow first-order kinetics, the concentration-time curve shows an exponential decrease in the plasma drug concentration over time and a linear decrease in drug concentration on logarithmic scale (see Fig. 47.5). The half-life of drug elimination is independent of drug dosage. Most drugs used in neonates follow first-order kinetic properties, including ampicillin, gentamicin, and phenobarbital.
paragraphs.heading: First-Order or Zero-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: Rarely, drugs may follow what is called zero-order kinetics or, nonlinear, saturable kinetics. In drugs that follow zeroorder kinetics, a constant amount of drug is metabolized or eliminated per unit of time regardless of concentration. The drug concentration follows a linear decrease of serum concentration over time (see Fig. 47.4). The elimination rate constant (Kel) is highly variable, with a smaller percentage of the drug eliminated at the beginning and a higher percentage of the residual drug eliminated toward the end, as demonstrated on a log-transformed scale. The half-life of drugs whose elimination follows zero-order kinetics is dependent on drug dosage;
paragraphs.heading: First-Order or Zero-Order Kinetics

paragraphs.text: larger doses yield a longer half-life. For example, after ingesting alcohol, the liver’s alcohol dehydrogenase quickly becomes saturated, such that only a fixed amount can be metabolized over a given amount of time. Small increases in dose can yield large increases in levels because the amount of drug removed is constant and not proportional to the dose. Phenytoin is another zero-order kinetic drug, owing to saturable kinetics of the metabolizing enzymes.14 Some drugs that typically follow first-order kinetics can follow zero-order kinetics when given at a very high dosage if enzymatic metabolism becomes saturated. When the drug concentrations decrease to the point that enzymatic reactions are no longer saturated, then first-order kinetics can resume.
paragraphs.heading: DRUG

paragraphs.text: The mathematical principles that describe the first-order kinetics of the dose-to-concentration relationship over time often use a compartmental approach to represent how a drug distributes through the body and the different rates of concentration changes in the body over time (see Fig. 47.5). In one-compartment models, a drug hypothetically distributes instantaneously in a homogeneous fashion into one compartment representing the entire body, and then the concentration declines linearly on a logarithmic scale with one rate constant (Kel) as the drug is eliminated. This simplified, one-compartment hypothetical model is most appropriate for
paragraphs.heading: One- Versus Two-Compartment Pharmacokinetic Models

paragraphs.text: drugs that are administered by fast infusion, rapidly distribute throughout the central compartment (short alpha phase), and have a relatively long beta phase of elimination that is the primary determinant of drug concentration over time (shown in dashed curve in one compartment example in Fig. 47.5).
paragraphs.heading: [C]

paragraphs.text: The two-compartment model is used to describe a drug with first-order kinetics that moves through the body in two distinct phases (see two-compartment model of Fig. 47.5). The alpha phase typically describes the drug’s initial distribution throughout the circulation with a relatively rapid rate of concentration decline, followed by the slower beta phase that describes the drug’s elimination from the body, in which drug concentrations decline more slowly. Two different exponential rates of decay are demonstrated by the change of slope in the semi-logarithmic plot of a concentration versus time. The distribution and elimination properties of widely distributed drugs that enter and exit numerous compartments often require multi-compartment models. The mathematical principles underlying multicompartment models are beyond the scope of this chapter.
paragraphs.heading: [C]

paragraphs.text: In neonates, developmental changes in body composition, renal and hepatic function, and pathophysiology with
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: clinical disease, can affect PK characteristics of drugs, specifically Vd and CL.1–3 Much of the variation in Vd across varying gestational ages and postnatal ages can be explained by differences in body composition. Neonates have higher proportions of extracellular and total body water compared with older infants and children. Preterm infants have the highest amount of total body water. Therefore hydrophilic drugs that distribute in water have a larger Vd in newborns, and even a larger Vd in preterm newborns. Infants with larger Vd will have lower peak drug concentrations unless they receive a higher dose. Infants with excess extracellular fluid, such as those with ascites or hydrops, can also have a large Vd for hydrophilic drugs.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: For lipophilic drugs, the body composition of fat can affect drug distribution into adipose tissue. If more drug is sequestered in fat, then plasma drug concentrations will be lower, Vd will be higher, and even the drug elimination characteristics (CL) can be affected because drug sequestered in fat is less available for elimination. Very preterm infants with minimal body fat will have a smaller Vd and less storage of lipophilic drugs (e.g., benzodiazepines, fentanyl) in peripheral fat; whereas large-for-gestational-age infants born to diabetic mothers can sequester lipophilic drugs in their peripheral tissue, thereby exhibiting larger Vd and lower plasma drug concentration.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Infants with low protein stores will have a greater proportion of free drug for a given total plasma drug concentration. The free drug component is the pharmacologically active moiety and may be more likely to distribute into peripheral tissues (larger Vd). The increased proportion of free or unbound drug can also contribute to faster elimination and a shorter half-life because free or unbound drug is more available for drug excretion mechanisms. However, the higher proportion of active, unbound drug relative to total drug concentration could explain toxicity at a similar total drug concentration. Neonates can also have a higher proportion of free drug compared with older infants because of endogenous competitors of protein binding, such as bilirubin or free fatty acids.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Age-dependent differences in drug binding in tissues can also affect distribution. Drugs can have extraordinarily large Vd if they are bound to proteins in the peripheral tissues. The disposition of these drugs through the body typically requires a two- or three-compartment model to account for the transfer of drug in and out of peripheral tissues (see Fig. 47.5). For example, digoxin has low plasma concentration and very large Vd; the drug is bound to proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle and thus sequestered in the peripheral tissue.15 Infants and children have increased myocardial uptake of digoxin, partially explaining the higher Vd in infants.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: At birth, elimination of drugs through the kidney is inefficient, leading to delayed drug CL and a prolonged half-life of many drugs. Renal elimination is limited by renal blood flow and the functional immaturity of the kidney, specifically glomerular filtration and tubular capacity for secretion and reabsorption. Glomerular filtration of drugs is dependent on renal blood flow and protein binding of the drug in
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: plasma. Drugs bound to proteins are typically too large to pass through glomeruli. Tubular secretion and reabsorption of drugs involve transport processes that are impacted by prematurity yet remain incompletely understood.2,3
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: For drugs with renal elimination, dose adjustment is often necessary to account for changes in renal CL associated with prematurity, postnatal age, and GFR. Hemodynamic changes after birth lead to increased renal blood flow and rapid changes in GFR over the first week after birth. Glomerular filtration is decreased in preterm infants, and although the GFR increases after birth, its increase does not match the increased GFR seen in term infants. In 3-day-old neonates, mean GFR increased significantly with advancing gestational age from 24 through 37 weeks.16 In preterm infants, the GFR has a significant increase occurring around 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Some of the differences in drug CL may reflect an infant’s stage of nephrogenesis, a process that is not complete until at least 36 weeks post-menstrual age.17 Preterm infants are at risk of having a decreased nephrogenic potential, which may contribute to decrease in drug CL. Delayed renal CL in the youngest, most immature infants can lead to high plasma drug concentration.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Many PK studies consider biomarkers that can predict renal elimination. Although many studies use serum creatinine (Scr) to guide drug dosing and adjustments in neonates, there are significant differences in Scr values for preterm and term infants. The Scr in preterm infants reflects the state of nephrogenesis until its completion at 35 to 36 weeks gestation and subsequently exhibits dynamic alterations over time. Scr levels often increase immediately after birth because of transient reabsorption across immature tubules and then decrease in the second week of life with maturation of glomerular filtration and tubular function. Scr requires time to accumulate in plasma. Subtle changes in urine output and GFR can result in decreased CL of renally eliminated drugs before detection of an elevated Scr.18 Clinicians must be aware of this delay in the rise of Scr levels in infants with acute kidney injury and consider empiric dose adjustments.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Scr has been an unreliable marker of renal function to predict alterations in the PK of drugs, and other biomarkers are being evaluated, including cystatin-C, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), and KIM-1. Cystatin-C is a cysteine protease inhibitor that is synthesized by all nucleated cells, filtered by the glomeruli, and metabolized by the proximal renal tubule cells. Because cystatin- C depends only on GFR, it rises more rapidly than Scr when GFR decreases and may be a better predictor for dose adjustments.19 Compared to Scr in term infants, cystatin- C more reliably predicted serum vancomycin concentrations.20 NGAL is expressed in neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages as an innate mediator of immune response, and it can be measured in urine to predict early stages of acute kidney injury. KIM-1 is a transmembrane glycoprotein that is detected in the urine only in the setting of acute kidney injury and is associated with increased mortality risk in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.21 These potential
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: biomarkers of renal function could be helpful in predicting changes in GFR that warrant dose adjustments. More PK studies are needed to validate the use of these biomarkers.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Infants with significant renal disease have changes in drug disposition beyond those expected by a reduction in GFR. Infants with significant renal disease often have electrolyte abnormalities that can affect the serum pH, which, in turn, affects the ionization state of drug molecules. Additionally, organic acids can accumulate in the plasma and compete with protein-bound drugs for albumin binding, thereby altering the Vd and availability of free drug for renal CL. An alteration in the pH of tubular fluid also affects the ionization state of a drug molecule, which, in turn, can affect tubular reabsorption.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Patients with liver disease or hepatic congestion often accumulate active drugs owing to their diminished metabolic capabilities and decreased first-pass metabolism. Patients with liver disease typically have low albumin or altered glycoprotein levels that may affect fractional protein binding of drugs, thereby altering the availability of free drug and Vd. Slow gut motility or bowel wall edema can impair enteral absorption.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Patients with cardiac dysfunction can exhibit altered perfusion, edema, hepatic congestion, and/or decreased renal perfusion. All phases of drug disposition (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and changes in PK properties of Vd and CL can be affected. Altered tissue perfusion and increased total body water, as seen in cardiac, renal, or hepatic dysfunction, can unpredictably alter Vd and CL based on patient physiology and drug-specific properties.
paragraphs.heading: Body Composition and Organ Function

paragraphs.text: Neonatal hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is often accompanied by metabolic acidemia in the first postnatal hours to days, along with kidney and liver injury. Therapeutic hypothermia is the standard treatment for late preterm or term neonates with a perinatal event concerning HIE. Therapeutic hypothermia involves decreasing the core body temperature below 34° C for the first 72 postnatal hours, followed by gradual rewarming.22 The combination of end organ injury and cooling below the physiologic core body temperature influences the PK of drugs.23 The severity of disease may be an important covariate of drug CL, and close monitoring of drug concentrations is important in these infants.24
paragraphs.heading: Therapeutic Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: Many drugs used in newborns undergoing therapeutic hypothermia have significantly altered PK profiles with reduced metabolism, lower CL, and prolonged half-lives that are attributed to both organ dysfunction incurred during perinatal asphyxia as well as the additive effects of hypothermia. Organ dysfunction, particularly renal and hepatic impairment because of decreased cardiac output and perfusion, results in decreased total body CL for commonly used drugs, such as antimicrobials, antiepileptics, and analgesics. Ampicillin, gentamicin, phenobarbital, and morphine have been reported to have delayed drug CL during therapeutic
paragraphs.heading: Therapeutic Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: hypothermia, and dose adjustments have been proposed to prevent toxicity.25–28 In adults treated with hypothermia, the systemic CL of hepatic cytochrome P450-metabolized drugs is decreased between 7% and 22% per degree Celsius below 37° C.29 The effect may be similar in neonates; however, the isoenzyme-specific ontogeny has not been fully studied in infants undergoing therapeutic hypothermia.30
paragraphs.heading: Therapeutic Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: Therapeutic drug monitoring helps achieve optimal doses while also minimizing risk of adverse effects in real time.31 Therapeutic drug monitoring is particularly useful for patients with changes in renal or hepatic function, patients undergoing therapeutic hypothermia treatments, and for medications with narrow therapeutic index. For infants undergoing therapeutic hypothermia, the dynamic changes in renal perfusion and GFR expected shortly after birth, the gradual improvements in organ function that occurs with clinical stability, and the changes in body temperature with rewarming all influence the PK of commonly used drugs. Studies have shown that phenobarbital, which is metabolized in the liver mostly by CYP2C9, has a prolonged half-life of 8 to 22 days in patients undergoing therapeutic hypothermia versus 4.3 days in term infants and 5.9 days in preterm infants without therapeutic hypothermia.28,32 Increased exposure to phenobarbital has been associated with worse neurodevelopmental outcomes, and therapeutic drug monitoring helps to ensure that phenobarbital doses are appropriately adjusted. Gentamicin also exhibits a decrease in CL and a longer half-life in cooled infants. Therapeutic drug monitoring for aminoglycosides is used to target therapeutic exposures for efficacy and minimize the risk of nephrotoxicity and hearing impairment.33 The decrease in CL and a longer half-life of gentamicin in cooling infants mandates spacing out dosing intervals to every 36 hours to prevent accumulation and high trough concentrations, rather than the standard dosing of every 24 hours.26
paragraphs.heading: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring During Therapeutic Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: Many drugs do not have assays available locally for therapeutic drug monitoring. Understanding the PK principles of drugs administered to newborns undergoing therapeutic hypothermia is critical to ensuring that the adverse effects of high drug concentrations do not negatively affect the recovery process. Midazolam and morphine, which are both metabolized in the liver by CYP3A and UDP-glucurono syltransferase 2B7, respectively, and renally eliminated, have prolonged half-lives and reduced CL during hypothermia treatment for HIE.27,34 High concentrations of morphine or midazolam can lead to adverse effects, such as hypotension, respiratory depression, and sedation.35,36 During hypothermia, morphine CL was found to be decreased by 20.7% and metabolites morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glu curonide decreased by 14.7%.27 To prevent morphine accumulation, the authors recommended a loading dose followed by a low-dose maintenance infusion. In refractory seizures, midazolam can be used in combination with phenobarbital.
paragraphs.heading: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring During Therapeutic Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: Phenobarbital is an inducer of CYP3A; therefore it can increase the CL of midazolam. A higher midazolam dose may be needed to maintain effective concentrations when used concomitantly with CYP3A inducers like phenobarbital. In contrast, if midazolam is used without phenobarbital, then the dose of midazolam may be reduced.34
paragraphs.heading: Therapeutic Drug Monitoring During Therapeutic Hypothermia

paragraphs.text: Basic PK principles can guide clinicians in how to use drug concentrations derived from therapeutic drug monitoring to determine appropriate dosing for an individual infant. This bedside PK approach, albeit simplified, is appropriate for many drugs used in newborns. Drug concentrations at different time points are used to derive infant-specific Vd, CL, Kel, and T1⁄2. These infant-specific PK parameters can then be used to determine what dose modifications are needed to achieve the desired drug concentrations over time for that specific infant (see Table 47.1). (For a more thorough explanation, see references1,6.)
paragraphs.heading: Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

paragraphs.text: This approach is most appropriate when the PK properties of the drug follow first-order kinetics and can be approximated by a one-compartment model. These simplified formulas can provide good estimates if the drug has a rapid distribution phase followed by a long beta phase of elimination, when therapeutic drug monitoring occurs during the elimination phase, and when the drug is administered with a short infusion time and long dosing intervals (see Fig. 47.5). In these scenarios, the drug concentrations at a given time after infusion are primarily impacted by the prolonged elimination beta phase.
paragraphs.heading: Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

paragraphs.text: This simplified approach of a one-compartment model is appropriate for gentamicin. Gentamicin PK properties (Vd, Kel, T1⁄2, and CL) can be estimated using a peak level obtained 30 minutes after the end of drug infusion, when equilibrium is expected to be established in circulation, and a trough level obtained before the next dose. The peak level will be somewhat lower than if measured at the end of the infusion. However, by obtaining the peak concentration 30 minutes after the end of infusion, there can be two drug concentrations (peak and trough) within the beta phase of elimination to allow calculation of Kel. The elimination rate constant (Kel) represents the slope of the line (change in concentration per change in time) on a log plot as shown in Table 47.1, Eq. [4a].
paragraphs.heading: Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

paragraphs.text: The peak concentration achieved from the dose of gentamicin is used to estimate Vd. In simplest terms, the Vd is the amount of drug infused divided by the amount of drug measured in the plasma. If 4 mg/kg is given and 10 mg/L is measured in the blood, then the Vd is 0.4 L/kg (see Table 47.1, Eq. [3a]). This Vd is slightly larger than would be predicted if peak was obtained at the end of infusion. This small difference is likely insignificant in the effort to target a therapeutic peak concentration. For precise calculation of Vd, one would use calculations that incorporate time of infusion and time after end of infusion (see Table 47.1, Eqs. [7, 10]).
paragraphs.heading: Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

paragraphs.text: The half-life (T1⁄2) is the time it takes to reduce the drug concentration (C) in half as shown in Eq. [5a], Table 47.1, and relates to the slope (elimination rate constant Kel) of concentration time curve on a semi-logarithmic plot. Halflife can be estimated from the drug concentration time curve (see Fig. 47.5) or from the elimination rate constant (0.693/Kel) or Vd and CL (see Table 47.1, Eq. [5]).
paragraphs.heading: Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

paragraphs.text: CL is a measure of the rate of drug elimination from the body. CL is formally defined as the volume of blood from which all drug is removed per unit of time. CL can be calculated using Vd and Kel (see Table 47.1, Eq. [6]). At steady state, drug input is equal to drug elimination; therefore the dose given (dose/interval) is equal to the amount of drug removed (CL × drug concentration at steady state) (see Table 47.1, Eq. [6c]).
paragraphs.heading: Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

paragraphs.text: In special circumstances in which drugs are infused over long time periods, the maximal concentration of drug measured at the end of infusion may be lower than expected and may overestimate the Vd. The lower Cmax is because the drug is being eliminated during the same time it is being infused. In this case, more complicated exponential equations would be necessary to estimate the Vd while taking drug elimination into account (see Table 47.1, Eqs. [7, 8, 9, 10]). The concentration of drug at the end of infusion (Cmax) is derived using the rate of the infusion (R0 defined as dose mg/kg divided by the time of infusion tinf), the CL, and the fraction of drug removed during the infusion time (see Table 47.1, Eq. [7]). If the peak concentration is obtained 30 minutes after the end of the infusion to allow for equilibrium after rapid distribution phase, then multiply Cmax by the decay factor (e−kt where t = 0.5 hour) to predict this peak level at the time used in therapeutic drug monitoring (see Table 47.1, Eq. [8]). Clinicians can predict the concentration at any time relative to Cmax at the end of infusion by adjusting the time parameter t in the decay factor (e−kt) (see Table 47.1, Eq. [8]). Because CL is derived from the ratio of Vd and Kel, this equation can be rearranged to calculate Vd while considering drug loss owing to elimination during infusion time (see Table 47.1, Eq. [9]). For calculations during continuous infusions, it is wise to consult a clinical pharmacist.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacokinetic Calculations Accounting for Infusion Time

paragraphs.text: Fortunately, most drugs in the NICU are administered IV over short (≤60 minutes) infusion times. These infusion times are short compared with the slow drug elimination rate and longer dosing intervals. Only a very small quantity of drug is eliminated during the actual infusion, allowing the use of simplified calculations.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacokinetic Calculations Accounting for Infusion Time

paragraphs.text: Therapeutic drug monitoring often takes place after multiple doses have been administered. Different formulas can be used that incorporate both the dosing interval, referred
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacokinetic Calculations After Multiple Doses

paragraphs.text: to as tau (τ), and the number of doses (n). If multiple doses have been administered, but it is not known if steady-state has been reached, then formulas allow for calculation of Cmax after n doses. Once Cmax is determined, then the decay factor (e−kt’) allows for calculation of drug concentration at time t after the nth dose (see Table 47.1, Eqs. [11, 12, 13]). Once at steady-state, CL can be determined from the dose, interval, and average steady-state drug concentration (see Table 47.1, Eq. [6c]).
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacokinetic Calculations After Multiple Doses

paragraphs.text: The PD of a drug explains the relationship between the concentration of a drug in the blood and the biochemical and physiologic effect of that drug on the body.2,4,5 The effect of a drug can relate to either its efficacy or adverse effects. The PD properties are drug specific, because they reflect their mechanism of action, potency, desired effect, and/or toxicity profile. Many drugs, such as dopamine, bind to physiologic receptors; agonists mimic the effects of endogenous ligands, whereas antagonists block the effects of endogenous ligands. The PD of receptor-binding drugs is altered during development because of changes in receptor binding, receptor density, and downstream signal transduction. Disease states, maturity, and concomitant medications can also alter drug PD.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: When clinical trials do not show desired efficacy, then one needs to reconsider the dose-exposure-response paradigm presented in Fig. 47.1. Lack of efficacy may be caused by the dose being too small and subtherapeutic concentrations. Alternatively, the dose may have achieved the desired concentration, but in the young infant, the plasma concentration did not correlate with the desired response.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: PD principles are well established for the treatment of infections.4,5 Antimicrobial drugs target the pathogen; therefore the exposure targets for bacterial or fungal eradication are likely to be appropriate across diverse age groups.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: Most infants in a NICU receive an antimicrobial drug; therefore it is worth reviewing the PK/PD paradigms that guide drug dosing for the effective treatment of infections.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: The goals of antimicrobial therapy are simple: eradicate the pathogen, minimize toxicity, and prevent emergence of resistant organisms (see Fig. 47.1). Once a drug has been chosen, the hard part is choosing the right dosing strategy to accomplish these goals. The PK properties of a drug, specifically the CL, Kel, T1⁄2, and Vd, explain the relationship between dose and concentration. PD tells us what concentration is necessary to kill the organism and reduce the risk of emerging resistance based upon human, animal, and in vitro studies. Optimal treatment of infections requires clinicians to incorporate these PK/PD principles (see Fig. 47.1) and use doses of antimicrobial drugs designed to meet PK/PD exposure targets.4,5 The concentration of the drug in the plasma is just one important aspect of treatment. Infant factors such as immunocompetence, bacterial load, and drug concentration at the site of infection are also important, but difficult to modify.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: Two important determinants of effective antimicrobial therapy are the drug exposure profile and the minimal inhibitory concentration (MIC) of a given organism (Fig. 47.6).4,5 The drug concentration curve demonstrates three important measures of exposure: (1) the maximal concentration referred to as Cmax or peak; (2) the area under the concentration curve (AUC), which refers to a measure of total drug exposure; and (3) the time or percent of dosing interval that the drug concentration is maintained above the MIC of the organism (% time). Effective therapy means optimizing this concentration curve relative to the MIC as illustrated by the three PK/PD exposure targets: Cmax/MIC, AUC/MIC, and %T > MIC.4,5
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: These three PK/PD exposure targets guide effective treatment.4,5 Antimicrobial drugs can be classified into three major categories: concentration-dependent killing, timedependent killing, and time-dependent killing with some
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: moderate persistent effects (Table 47.2). Gentamicin is concentration dependent; therefore the higher the dose, the higher the Cmax, and the more killing is achieved. Gentamicin also has a significant post-antibacterial effect, meaning that the higher the Cmax, the more bacterial growth is subsequently suppressed after levels decrease. Beta-lactam antibiotics, such as ampicillin, are not concentration dependent; efficacy is associated with the percent of time that the concentration is maintained above the MIC. For ampicillin, effective bacterial killing starts to occur when levels are twofold greater than MIC. Increasing ampicillin concentration to more than fourfold MIC does not decrease the bacterial burden. Ampicillin has no postexposure antibacterial activity, so bacterial growth can occur when concentrations are below the MIC. Beta-lactam antibiotics require more frequent dosing or prolonged infusion time to sustain drug levels above the MIC for at least 50% of the dosing interval. Finally, bacterial killing with vancomycin is independent of concentration; however, there is a modest post-antibacterial effect such that higher concentrations (AUC) are associated with prolonged killing even as levels decrease. Vancomycin efficacy is associated with the AUC/MIC exposure target. Antimicrobial drug dosing guidelines are designed to optimize these PK/PD exposure targets.37 All exposure targets are relative to the MIC. Therefore the higher the MIC, the harder it is to achieve the exposure target, even if the MIC is within the sensitive range for that drug.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: When approaching drug choice and dosage, it is necessary to consider factors that affect PK/PD target attainment and potential outcomes. Patient-specific factors such as maturity, organ function, and fluid status affect attainment of PK/PD targets. Pathogen-specific factors can determine virulence and drug susceptibility or resistance. Drug-specific factors such as tissue penetration, formulation, and the
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: availability of PK information in neonates are also important. Finally, the ability to achieve adequate drug concentration at the site of infection can affect outcomes. Neonates are notorious for their susceptibility to meningitis and severe abdominal infections associated with ascites and large fluid shifts. Clinical disease states affect the disposition and PK of drugs in patients.
paragraphs.heading: Pharmacodynamics

paragraphs.text: Clinicians can use the formulas in Table 47.1 to perform simple calculations to estimate an individual infant’s Vd, CL, Kel, and T1⁄2 and then to determine dose modification for that individual infant.1,6 To demonstrate the use of these formulas, the extended-interval dosing of gentamicin in three newborns of varied gestational age is reviewed (Box 47.1). Gentamicin serves as one of the best examples of PK/ PD-derived dosing guidelines for neonates across the gestational age spectrum. Gentamicin exhibits concentrationdependent killing.4,5 Optimal efficacy is achieved when the ratio of gentamicin peak concentration over MIC is at least 10 mg/L.33 In adults, once-daily high-dose regimens have shown enhanced efficacy with less toxicity. Decreased renal toxicity is attributed to the reduction in renal drug accumulation, because the uptake of drug into the kidney becomes saturated at high concentrations (saturable drug uptake).38 The extended interval allows for appropriate washout. In the examples found in Box 47.1A–C, Mary, Jack, and Ava are three newborns who all receive gentamicin as empiric coverage for early-onset sepsis.

47 Pharmacokinetics in Neonatal Medicine

### CHI D. HORNIK AND KELLY C. WADE

The safe and effective use of medications in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) requires an understanding of the principles of pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD) that guide individual dosing and aim to provide drug exposures designed for the best clinical outcomes and lowest risk of adverse effects. Significant differences in neonatal physiology affect drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination. Therefore the PK of drugs in neonates is unique and cannot be extrapolated from older children or adults (for excellent comprehensive reviews see references 1–3).1–3 Biologic variation among infants in the NICU is extensive: infant’s weight varies at least 10-fold (0.5–5 kg), gestational age at birth varies between 22 and 42 weeks, and postnatal age typically ranges from 1 to 150 days. Infants are undergoing dramatic changes in body size, body composition, cardiac output and perfusion, renal and hepatic function, and ontogeny (agerelated maturation) of drug metabolizing enzymes. This means that infants in the NICU will exhibit wide variations in drug exposures, and care providers often need to consider dose adjustments. Developmental changes in organ systems also influence safety and efficacy of drugs used in infants. Basic knowledge of PK and PD can explain rational dosing across a broad spectrum of prematurity, clinical conditions, treatment interventions, and drug classes. The interplay of PK and PD relationships allows clinicians to target specific drug concentrations that have been associated with therapeutic efficacy (Fig. 47.1).

Anti-infective drugs are the most common class of drugs used in the NICU and provide a useful context to understand basic principles of PK and PD (see Fig. 47.1). The goals of antimicrobial therapy are simple: eradicate the pathogen, minimize toxicity, and prevent emergence of resistant organisms.4,5 The PK of a drug explains the dose-concentration relationship, whereas the PD of a drug explains the relationship between the concentration of the drug in the body and the therapeutic or toxic response. ### Drug Disposition Explains Drug Exposure Over Time: Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, and Excretion

Drug disposition describes how drugs enter and exit the body and explains how concentrations in the body change

over time (Figs. 47.2 and 47.3). Four basic processes explain the disposition of drugs through the body: absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. These processes are affected by chemical properties of the drug, patient-specific physiology, body composition, developmental maturation, and pathophysiology relating to disease state. Applying PK principles in neonates requires an understanding of drug disposition and the impact of both developmental pharmacology and patient-specific physiology.1–3

### Drug Absorption and Route of Drug Administration

Absorption specifically refers to the process of drug transfer from its site of administration to the bloodstream (see Fig. 47.2). Drugs typically enter the body via intravenous (IV), enteral (per oral, PO), intramuscular (IM), intrapulmonary, subcutaneous, or percutaneous routes and are then absorbed into the circulation as free drug. The route of administration affects the concentration of the drug over time (see Fig. 47.3). Bioavailability of a drug refers to the fraction of the administered dose that reaches the circulation but does not consider the rate of drug absorption. Bioavailability is determined by comparing the respective areas under the plasma concentration curves (AUC) after a non- IV form of administration with the AUC after an IV administration. IV administration of a drug, with the exception of dosing formulations of prodrugs, provides the most consistent, reliable absorption into the circulation and therefore defines a bioavailability of 100%. Neonates have unique absorption properties that impact drug concentrations after enteral administration.1–3 Although the ontogeny of gastric acid production and secretion is not fully understood, neonates with reduced gastric acidity have increased absorption of acid-labile molecules (penicillin) and decreased absorption of weak organic acids (phenytoin, phenobarbital). Frequent and continuous oral feedings in infants may result in higher gastric pH and impact the absorption of these drugs. Slower gastric emptying time and intestinal motility among preterm infants can change the time to absorb the drug and amount of drug absorbed. Enteral absorption often improves as infants become older. Absorption of enteral medications is often decreased in infants with GI pathology or changes in perfusion to the GI system. Anticipating differences in bioavailability helps guide dose adjustment when converting between IV and PO routes of administration.

Bioavailability after IM and percutaneous (topical or transdermal) administration can be affected by tissue mass, perfusion, drug permeability, and surface area. In neonates, reduced muscle perfusion and contractility can limit absorption after IM administration.3 The percutaneous absorption of the drug is directly related to the degree of skin hydration and relative surface area and inversely related to the thickness of the stratum corneum. Percutaneous application of medications in preterm infants can lead to large systemic drug exposures given their increased skin perfusion secondary to larger surface area, higher water content, and thin stratum corneum.

### Drug Distribution and Volume of Distribution

Distribution refers to the process by which drugs move from the central circulation through various compartments and peripheral tissues in the body according to physiochemical properties such as the molecular size, ionization constant, and relative hydrophilic/lipophilic properties (see Fig. 47.2). The central compartment typically refers to the vascular space with rapid distribution to the heart, kidney, and liver. From the central compartment, drugs distribute at a slower rate to the peripheral compartment(s), which can include brain, fat, and muscle. From the peripheral tissues, drugs traverse back into the central compartment to be eliminated. Drug distribution depends on drug-specific factors (molecular size, ionization constant, relative hydrophilic/ lipophilic properties, protein binding) and infant-specific factors (body composition, membrane/tissue permeability, cardiac output). Distribution is an important concept to understanding PK because it relates to the maximum drug

concentration after a given dose and the volume of distribution (Vd). The kinetics of drug transfer to and from the peripheral and central compartments also affects the kinetics of drug excretion and the shape of the drug concentration curve over time.

The apparent Vd for a drug is defined as the hypothetical fluid volume through which the drug is dispersed. It is calculated by dividing the total amount of drug given by the concentration of drug in plasma (Table 47.1, Eq. [3]). This proportionality constant links the dose of the drug to the measured concentration in that compartment. Vd does not refer to any physiologic compartment or the blood volume. Instead, Vd relates to the hypothetical volume of the total compartment that explains the concentration of the drug achieved after administering a given amount.

Vd is one of the most important parameters of the PK of drugs and is a major factor in determining drug exposure after a given dose.2,3 Understanding the factors that contribute to variation in Vd is helpful in determining the optimal dose of a medication to achieve a desired peak concentration (Cmax) in a specific patient. An infant with a higher Vd will have a lower peak concentration of drug in circulation. High Vd can indicate that the infant has an increase in total body water and extracellular fluid or that the drug has a wide distribution to peripheral tissues where it might be sequestered. Gentamicin is a highly polar, hydrophilic molecule that distributes readily in extracellular fluid. Relative to term infants, preterm infants have a higher body water content and therefore require a higher dose of gentamicin per their body weight to achieve the same peak concentration as a term infant.

Plasma protein binding can have significant effects on distribution. Drugs that exhibit high protein-binding capacity often have smaller Vd because they bind to plasma proteins and are maintained in the circulation. Protein binding is also affected by availability of binding proteins, differences of binding capacity among different proteins, and increases in bilirubin or free fatty acids that can reduce drug protein binding. Drugs that remain unbound to proteins (“free” drugs) are not only pharmacologically active but also more available for metabolism and/or elimination. Neonates typically have a higher proportion of “free drug” compared to total drug because of decreased concentrations of albumin, alpha-1 acid glycoprotein, and plasma globulins compared to adults.2,3 Lower amounts of these binding proteins can result in toxicities associated with higher free drug concentrations. Increased concentrations of bilirubin and free fatty acids can also increase the amount of “free drug” because they compete with drugs for protein binding.

Hepatic processes change rapidly over the first month, so dose adjustment is often necessary with advancing postnatal and postmenstrual age. Fentanyl is metabolized by hepatic CYP3A4-mediated N-dealkylation to norfentanyl. Fentanyl elimination depends on liver blood flow, hepatic uptake, and CYP3A4 activity. Understanding the differences in drug metabolism is important to knowing drug exposures in neonates; if neonates cannot effectively metabolize a drug, then higher concentrations of the active drug can potentiate effects

of the drug or lead to toxicity. In the absence of specific drug-metabolizing enzymes, neonates may use alternative pathways and produce different metabolites with different activity or toxicity profiles. As drug-metabolizing capacity improves with age, higher doses are necessary to achieve desired concentration and response.

### Drug Excretion

The excretion of active drugs or their metabolites is the process by which drugs are removed from the body. Drug excretion primarily occurs through the kidney and liver (see Fig. 47.2).1–3 The kidney uses three mechanisms of drug excretion: glomerular filtration, active secretion through the proximal tubules, or distal tubule reabsorption. Glomerular filtration is very low in the first few days after birth and increases with hemodynamic changes and improved renal perfusion. Glomerular filtration also increases with gestational age; preterm infants typically have delayed renal CL and a longer half-life compared with term infants.1–3 Disease states common in critically ill newborns, such as neonatal encephalopathy, sepsis, acute kidney injury, and congenital heart disease, all have been associated with reduced glomerular filtration and reduced drug excretion.

Tubular processes related to drug secretion and reabsorption are also important to renal elimination, yet incompletely understood, particularly in neonates. Drug secretion in the proximal tubules uses transport systems that typically eliminate organic anions. Secretion transporter proteins secrete drugs that are conjugated with glucuronic acid, glycine, and sulfate, such as penicillin or furosemide. Tubular secretion is less developed in newborns, thereby partially explaining the prolonged half-life of penicillin and furosemide.1–3 Membrane transporters in the distal tubule can actively reabsorb drugs from the tubular lumen back into the systemic circulation. Tubular reabsorption is also delayed in neonates. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) typically improves with maturation faster than tubular mechanisms.

The liver uses four mechanisms of drug excretion: drug metabolism, excretion into bile, fecal elimination, and enterohepatic recirculation. Hepatic drug elimination can be dependent on hepatic blood flow and the metabolic capacity of liver. Patients with hepatic insufficiency have decreased elimination of drugs because of alterations in protein levels and protein binding, decreased liver blood flow, decreased uptake into hepatocytes, and altered hepatic enzymatic reaction. Patients with hepatic insufficiency, however, exhibit marked variability in drug metabolism and elimination. Infants with hepatic insufficiency typically benefit from lower doses of drugs that are eliminated by hepatic biotransformation and therapeutic drug monitoring when possible.

Regardless of excretion mechanism, the rate at which drugs are eliminated from the circulation is essential to the PK properties of drug CL, elimination rate constant (Kel), and half-life (T1⁄2) (see formulas in Table 47.1, Eqs. [4, 6]). Drug CL is defined as the volume of blood from which all drug is removed per unit time; Kel represents the elimination

CL can be affected by body weight, body surface area, cardiac output, hepatic function, renal function, plasma protein binding, concomitant medications, and variation in the expression of drug metabolizing enzymes. At steady state, drug input is equal to drug elimination and therefore the dose given (dose/interval) is equal to the amount of drug removed (CL × drug concentration at steady state).

### Drug Disposition Impacts Pharmacokinetic Characteristics of Drugs in Neonates

Drug disposition (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) exhibits marked complexity and interpatient variability in neonates given the infant’s specific differences in body size and composition, maturation, postnatal age, organ function, and clinical disease (pathophysiology).1–3 In neonates, the Vd is often higher for hydrophilic drugs, leading to a lower maximum drug concentration. Elimination (Kel) and CL are often slower because of reduced rates of biotransformation and renal elimination. The expected changes in drug metabolism with maturation can be highly variable and depend on the drug, the metabolic pathways, and clinical disease. The PK characteristics of drugs, specifically Vd and CL, need to be studied across a broad range of prematurity, body compositions, postnatal and postmenstrual ages, and disease states.

### First-Order or Zero-Order Kinetics

The drug-concentration-over-time graphs in Fig. 47.4 depict the rate of elimination of a drug from the body on a linear and semi-logarithmic plot. Most drugs follow firstorder kinetics, and mathematical equations in Table 47.1 are appropriate for drugs that are eliminated using properties of first-order kinetics.1,6 For drugs that follow first-order kinetics, a constant percentage of drug is metabolized over time. When drugs follow first-order kinetics, the concentration-time curve shows an exponential decrease in the plasma drug concentration over time and a linear decrease in drug concentration on logarithmic scale (see Fig. 47.5).
