### Important Factors That Impact Pharmacokinetics

### Body Composition and Organ Function

In neonates, developmental changes in body composition, renal and hepatic function, and pathophysiology with


## PDF page 800 | printed page 793

clinical disease, can affect PK characteristics of drugs, specifically Vd and CL.1–3 Much of the variation in Vd across varying gestational ages and postnatal ages can be explained by differences in body composition. Neonates have higher proportions of extracellular and total body water compared with older infants and children. Preterm infants have the highest amount of total body water. Therefore hydrophilic drugs that distribute in water have a larger Vd in newborns, and even a larger Vd in preterm newborns. Infants with larger Vd will have lower peak drug concentrations unless they receive a higher dose. Infants with excess extracellular fluid, such as those with ascites or hydrops, can also have a large Vd for hydrophilic drugs.

For lipophilic drugs, the body composition of fat can affect drug distribution into adipose tissue. If more drug is sequestered in fat, then plasma drug concentrations will be lower, Vd will be higher, and even the drug elimination characteristics (CL) can be affected because drug sequestered in fat is less available for elimination. Very preterm infants with minimal body fat will have a smaller Vd and less storage of lipophilic drugs (e.g., benzodiazepines, fentanyl) in peripheral fat; whereas large-for-gestational-age infants born to diabetic mothers can sequester lipophilic drugs in their peripheral tissue, thereby exhibiting larger Vd and lower plasma drug concentration.

Infants with low protein stores will have a greater proportion of free drug for a given total plasma drug concentration. The free drug component is the pharmacologically active moiety and may be more likely to distribute into peripheral tissues (larger Vd). The increased proportion of free or unbound drug can also contribute to faster elimination and a shorter half-life because free or unbound drug is more available for drug excretion mechanisms. However, the higher proportion of active, unbound drug relative to total drug concentration could explain toxicity at a similar total drug concentration. Neonates can also have a higher proportion of free drug compared with older infants because of endogenous competitors of protein binding, such as bilirubin or free fatty acids.

Age-dependent differences in drug binding in tissues can also affect distribution. Drugs can have extraordinarily large Vd if they are bound to proteins in the peripheral tissues. The disposition of these drugs through the body typically requires a two- or three-compartment model to account for the transfer of drug in and out of peripheral tissues (see Fig. 47.5). For example, digoxin has low plasma concentration and very large Vd; the drug is bound to proteins in skeletal and cardiac muscle and thus sequestered in the peripheral tissue.15 Infants and children have increased myocardial uptake of digoxin, partially explaining the higher Vd in infants.

At birth, elimination of drugs through the kidney is inefficient, leading to delayed drug CL and a prolonged half-life of many drugs. Renal elimination is limited by renal blood flow and the functional immaturity of the kidney, specifically glomerular filtration and tubular capacity for secretion and reabsorption. Glomerular filtration of drugs is dependent on renal blood flow and protein binding of the drug in

plasma. Drugs bound to proteins are typically too large to pass through glomeruli. Tubular secretion and reabsorption of drugs involve transport processes that are impacted by prematurity yet remain incompletely understood.2,3

For drugs with renal elimination, dose adjustment is often necessary to account for changes in renal CL associated with prematurity, postnatal age, and GFR. Hemodynamic changes after birth lead to increased renal blood flow and rapid changes in GFR over the first week after birth. Glomerular filtration is decreased in preterm infants, and although the GFR increases after birth, its increase does not match the increased GFR seen in term infants. In 3-day-old neonates, mean GFR increased significantly with advancing gestational age from 24 through 37 weeks.16 In preterm infants, the GFR has a significant increase occurring around 34 weeks’ postmenstrual age. Some of the differences in drug CL may reflect an infant’s stage of nephrogenesis, a process that is not complete until at least 36 weeks post-menstrual age.17 Preterm infants are at risk of having a decreased nephrogenic potential, which may contribute to decrease in drug CL. Delayed renal CL in the youngest, most immature infants can lead to high plasma drug concentration.

Many PK studies consider biomarkers that can predict renal elimination. Although many studies use serum creatinine (Scr) to guide drug dosing and adjustments in neonates, there are significant differences in Scr values for preterm and term infants. The Scr in preterm infants reflects the state of nephrogenesis until its completion at 35 to 36 weeks gestation and subsequently exhibits dynamic alterations over time. Scr levels often increase immediately after birth because of transient reabsorption across immature tubules and then decrease in the second week of life with maturation of glomerular filtration and tubular function. Scr requires time to accumulate in plasma. Subtle changes in urine output and GFR can result in decreased CL of renally eliminated drugs before detection of an elevated Scr.18 Clinicians must be aware of this delay in the rise of Scr levels in infants with acute kidney injury and consider empiric dose adjustments.

Scr has been an unreliable marker of renal function to predict alterations in the PK of drugs, and other biomarkers are being evaluated, including cystatin-C, neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalin (NGAL), and KIM-1. Cystatin-C is a cysteine protease inhibitor that is synthesized by all nucleated cells, filtered by the glomeruli, and metabolized by the proximal renal tubule cells. Because cystatin- C depends only on GFR, it rises more rapidly than Scr when GFR decreases and may be a better predictor for dose adjustments.19 Compared to Scr in term infants, cystatin- C more reliably predicted serum vancomycin concentrations.20 NGAL is expressed in neutrophils, monocytes, and macrophages as an innate mediator of immune response, and it can be measured in urine to predict early stages of acute kidney injury. KIM-1 is a transmembrane glycoprotein that is detected in the urine only in the setting of acute kidney injury and is associated with increased mortality risk in very low birth weight (VLBW) infants.21 These potential


## PDF page 801

biomarkers of renal function could be helpful in predicting changes in GFR that warrant dose adjustments. More PK studies are needed to validate the use of these biomarkers.

Infants with significant renal disease have changes in drug disposition beyond those expected by a reduction in GFR. Infants with significant renal disease often have electrolyte abnormalities that can affect the serum pH, which, in turn, affects the ionization state of drug molecules. Additionally, organic acids can accumulate in the plasma and compete with protein-bound drugs for albumin binding, thereby altering the Vd and availability of free drug for renal CL. An alteration in the pH of tubular fluid also affects the ionization state of a drug molecule, which, in turn, can affect tubular reabsorption.

Patients with liver disease or hepatic congestion often accumulate active drugs owing to their diminished metabolic capabilities and decreased first-pass metabolism. Patients with liver disease typically have low albumin or altered glycoprotein levels that may affect fractional protein binding of drugs, thereby altering the availability of free drug and Vd. Slow gut motility or bowel wall edema can impair enteral absorption.

Patients with cardiac dysfunction can exhibit altered perfusion, edema, hepatic congestion, and/or decreased renal perfusion. All phases of drug disposition (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and changes in PK properties of Vd and CL can be affected. Altered tissue perfusion and increased total body water, as seen in cardiac, renal, or hepatic dysfunction, can unpredictably alter Vd and CL based on patient physiology and drug-specific properties.

### Therapeutic Hypothermia

Neonatal hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is often accompanied by metabolic acidemia in the first postnatal hours to days, along with kidney and liver injury. Therapeutic hypothermia is the standard treatment for late preterm or term neonates with a perinatal event concerning HIE. Therapeutic hypothermia involves decreasing the core body temperature below 34° C for the first 72 postnatal hours, followed by gradual rewarming.22 The combination of end organ injury and cooling below the physiologic core body temperature influences the PK of drugs.23 The severity of disease may be an important covariate of drug CL, and close monitoring of drug concentrations is important in these infants.24

Many drugs used in newborns undergoing therapeutic hypothermia have significantly altered PK profiles with reduced metabolism, lower CL, and prolonged half-lives that are attributed to both organ dysfunction incurred during perinatal asphyxia as well as the additive effects of hypothermia. Organ dysfunction, particularly renal and hepatic impairment because of decreased cardiac output and perfusion, results in decreased total body CL for commonly used drugs, such as antimicrobials, antiepileptics, and analgesics. Ampicillin, gentamicin, phenobarbital, and morphine have been reported to have delayed drug CL during therapeutic

hypothermia, and dose adjustments have been proposed to prevent toxicity.25–28 In adults treated with hypothermia, the systemic CL of hepatic cytochrome P450-metabolized drugs is decreased between 7% and 22% per degree Celsius below 37° C.29 The effect may be similar in neonates; however, the isoenzyme-specific ontogeny has not been fully studied in infants undergoing therapeutic hypothermia.30

### Therapeutic Drug Monitoring During Therapeutic Hypothermia

Therapeutic drug monitoring helps achieve optimal doses while also minimizing risk of adverse effects in real time.31 Therapeutic drug monitoring is particularly useful for patients with changes in renal or hepatic function, patients undergoing therapeutic hypothermia treatments, and for medications with narrow therapeutic index. For infants undergoing therapeutic hypothermia, the dynamic changes in renal perfusion and GFR expected shortly after birth, the gradual improvements in organ function that occurs with clinical stability, and the changes in body temperature with rewarming all influence the PK of commonly used drugs. Studies have shown that phenobarbital, which is metabolized in the liver mostly by CYP2C9, has a prolonged half-life of 8 to 22 days in patients undergoing therapeutic hypothermia versus 4.3 days in term infants and 5.9 days in preterm infants without therapeutic hypothermia.28,32 Increased exposure to phenobarbital has been associated with worse neurodevelopmental outcomes, and therapeutic drug monitoring helps to ensure that phenobarbital doses are appropriately adjusted. Gentamicin also exhibits a decrease in CL and a longer half-life in cooled infants. Therapeutic drug monitoring for aminoglycosides is used to target therapeutic exposures for efficacy and minimize the risk of nephrotoxicity and hearing impairment.33 The decrease in CL and a longer half-life of gentamicin in cooling infants mandates spacing out dosing intervals to every 36 hours to prevent accumulation and high trough concentrations, rather than the standard dosing of every 24 hours.26

Many drugs do not have assays available locally for therapeutic drug monitoring. Understanding the PK principles of drugs administered to newborns undergoing therapeutic hypothermia is critical to ensuring that the adverse effects of high drug concentrations do not negatively affect the recovery process. Midazolam and morphine, which are both metabolized in the liver by CYP3A and UDP-glucurono syltransferase 2B7, respectively, and renally eliminated, have prolonged half-lives and reduced CL during hypothermia treatment for HIE.27,34 High concentrations of morphine or midazolam can lead to adverse effects, such as hypotension, respiratory depression, and sedation.35,36 During hypothermia, morphine CL was found to be decreased by 20.7% and metabolites morphine-3-glucuronide and morphine-6-glu curonide decreased by 14.7%.27 To prevent morphine accumulation, the authors recommended a loading dose followed by a low-dose maintenance infusion. In refractory seizures, midazolam can be used in combination with phenobarbital.

### Basic Pharmacokinetic Calculations for Clinicians

Basic PK principles can guide clinicians in how to use drug concentrations derived from therapeutic drug monitoring to determine appropriate dosing for an individual infant. This bedside PK approach, albeit simplified, is appropriate for many drugs used in newborns. Drug concentrations at different time points are used to derive infant-specific Vd, CL, Kel, and T1⁄2. These infant-specific PK parameters can then be used to determine what dose modifications are needed to achieve the desired drug concentrations over time for that specific infant (see Table 47.1). (For a more thorough explanation, see references1,6.)

This approach is most appropriate when the PK properties of the drug follow first-order kinetics and can be approximated by a one-compartment model. These simplified formulas can provide good estimates if the drug has a rapid distribution phase followed by a long beta phase of elimination, when therapeutic drug monitoring occurs during the elimination phase, and when the drug is administered with a short infusion time and long dosing intervals (see Fig. 47.5). In these scenarios, the drug concentrations at a given time after infusion are primarily impacted by the prolonged elimination beta phase.

This simplified approach of a one-compartment model is appropriate for gentamicin. Gentamicin PK properties (Vd, Kel, T1⁄2, and CL) can be estimated using a peak level obtained 30 minutes after the end of drug infusion, when equilibrium is expected to be established in circulation, and a trough level obtained before the next dose. The peak level will be somewhat lower than if measured at the end of the infusion. However, by obtaining the peak concentration 30 minutes after the end of infusion, there can be two drug concentrations (peak and trough) within the beta phase of elimination to allow calculation of Kel. The elimination rate constant (Kel) represents the slope of the line (change in concentration per change in time) on a log plot as shown in Table 47.1, Eq. [4a].

The peak concentration achieved from the dose of gentamicin is used to estimate Vd. In simplest terms, the Vd is the amount of drug infused divided by the amount of drug measured in the plasma. If 4 mg/kg is given and 10 mg/L is measured in the blood, then the Vd is 0.4 L/kg (see Table 47.1, Eq. [3a]). This Vd is slightly larger than would be predicted if peak was obtained at the end of infusion. This small difference is likely insignificant in the effort to target a therapeutic peak concentration. For precise calculation of Vd, one would use calculations that incorporate time of infusion and time after end of infusion (see Table 47.1, Eqs. [7, 10]).

The half-life (T1⁄2) is the time it takes to reduce the drug concentration (C) in half as shown in Eq. [5a], Table 47.1, and relates to the slope (elimination rate constant Kel) of concentration time curve on a semi-logarithmic plot. Halflife can be estimated from the drug concentration time curve (see Fig. 47.5) or from the elimination rate constant (0.693/Kel) or Vd and CL (see Table 47.1, Eq. [5]).

CL is a measure of the rate of drug elimination from the body. CL is formally defined as the volume of blood from which all drug is removed per unit of time. CL can be calculated using Vd and Kel (see Table 47.1, Eq. [6]). At steady state, drug input is equal to drug elimination; therefore the dose given (dose/interval) is equal to the amount of drug removed (CL × drug concentration at steady state) (see Table 47.1, Eq. [6c]).

### Pharmacokinetic Calculations Accounting for Infusion Time

In special circumstances in which drugs are infused over long time periods, the maximal concentration of drug measured at the end of infusion may be lower than expected and may overestimate the Vd. The lower Cmax is because the drug is being eliminated during the same time it is being infused. In this case, more complicated exponential equations would be necessary to estimate the Vd while taking drug elimination into account (see Table 47.1, Eqs. [7, 8, 9, 10]). [7]). If the peak concentration is obtained 30 minutes after the end of the infusion to allow for equilibrium after rapid distribution phase, then multiply Cmax by the decay factor (e−kt where t = 0.5 hour) to predict this peak level at the time used in therapeutic drug monitoring (see Table 47.1, Eq. [8]). Clinicians can predict the concentration at any time relative to Cmax at the end of infusion by adjusting the time parameter t in the decay factor (e−kt) (see Table 47.1, Eq. [8]). Because CL is derived from the ratio of Vd and Kel, this equation can be rearranged to calculate Vd while considering drug loss owing to elimination during infusion time (see Table 47.1, Eq. [9]). Fortunately, most drugs in the NICU are administered IV over short (≤60 minutes) infusion times. These infusion times are short compared with the slow drug elimination rate and longer dosing intervals. Only a very small quantity of drug is eliminated during the actual infusion, allowing the use of simplified calculations.

### Pharmacodynamics

The PD of a drug explains the relationship between the concentration of a drug in the blood and the biochemical and physiologic effect of that drug on the body.2,4,5 The effect of a drug can relate to either its efficacy or adverse effects. The PD properties are drug specific, because they reflect their mechanism of action, potency, desired effect, and/or toxicity profile. Many drugs, such as dopamine, bind to physiologic receptors; agonists mimic the effects of endogenous ligands, whereas antagonists block the effects of endogenous ligands. The PD of receptor-binding drugs is altered during development because of changes in receptor binding, receptor density, and downstream signal transduction. Disease states, maturity, and concomitant medications can also alter drug PD.

When clinical trials do not show desired efficacy, then one needs to reconsider the dose-exposure-response paradigm presented in Fig. 47.1. Lack of efficacy may be caused by the dose being too small and subtherapeutic concentrations. Alternatively, the dose may have achieved the desired concentration, but in the young infant, the plasma concentration did not correlate with the desired response.

PD principles are well established for the treatment of infections.4,5 Antimicrobial drugs target the pathogen; therefore the exposure targets for bacterial or fungal eradication are likely to be appropriate across diverse age groups.

The goals of antimicrobial therapy are simple: eradicate the pathogen, minimize toxicity, and prevent emergence of resistant organisms (see Fig. 47.1). One (A) and two (B) compartment models are shown with associated graphs of drug concentrations plotted over time on a linear (left) and semi-logarithmic (right) scale. A one-compartment model is a simplified, hypothetical example of a drug with instantaneous distribution. In reality (dashed line in A with peak measured 30 minutes after end of infusion), drugs that have a rapid distribution phase and longer elimination phase can approximate a one-compartment model, allowing the use of simplified formulas to calculate pharmacokinetic parameters. [Cmax] allows calculation of the volume of distribution (Vd). The drug concentration at any time t ([Ct]) can be calculated using Cmax and exponential decay factor (e−kt). Admin, Administration; C, drug concentration; Kel, elimination rate constant; T1⁄2, half-life.

• Fig. 47.6 Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) exposure targets guide optimal treatment of infections. This graph shows how a drug concentration changes over time after dose. The drug exposure is shown relative to potential minimal inhibitory concentrations (MIC) of an offending organism. Effective therapy meets one of three potential PK/PD exposure targets: Cmax/MIC, area under concentration curve (AUC)/MIC, and the %T > MIC (%T > MIC refers to the percent of dosing interval time, when the concentration of drug is above the MIC). As the MIC increases, the PK/PD exposure target becomes more difficult to obtain.
